why_correct: Carl Linnaeus introduced binomial nomenclature in Species Plantarum in 1753, giving every organism a two-word Latin name of genus and species. He is called the father of taxonomy.

why_wrong.0: Aristotle made the earliest known attempt at classification, dividing animals by habitat and blood, but he used no two-word naming system.
why_wrong.2: Robert Whittaker proposed the five kingdom classification in 1969, which is about grouping rather than naming.
why_wrong.3: Charles Darwin explained how species arise through natural selection. He used the naming system rather than inventing it.

why_correct: A herbarium is a store of plant specimens that have been dried, pressed and mounted on sheets, each with a label giving its name, place and date of collection. It is the reference collection a taxonomist works from.

why_wrong.0: A museum keeps preserved specimens of animals and plants generally, often in fluid or as skins, rather than pressed sheets.
why_wrong.1: A botanical garden grows living plants for study and display. Living, not dried, which is the key difference.
why_wrong.3: A zoological park keeps live animals.

why_correct: Mitosis is called equational division because each daughter cell ends with the same chromosome number as the parent. It is how growth and repair take place.

why_wrong.1: Meiosis I is the reductional division, in which the chromosome number is halved.
why_wrong.2: Meiosis II is equational in the sense that the number does not change again, but the cells entering it are already haploid, so it is not what this term names. The standard answer for equational division is mitosis.
why_wrong.3: Amitosis is direct division without spindle or visible chromosomes, seen in some simple cells.

why_correct: Crossing over takes place in pachytene, the third substage of prophase I. The homologous chromosomes are already paired, and the enzyme recombinase exchanges segments between non-sister chromatids.

why_wrong.0: In leptotene the chromosomes are only beginning to condense and have not yet paired, so there is nothing to cross over with.
why_wrong.1: In zygotene the homologues pair up through synapsis. Pairing is the preparation for crossing over, not the event itself.
why_wrong.3: In diplotene the paired chromosomes begin to separate and chiasmata become visible. Those chiasmata are the evidence that crossing over has already happened.

why_correct: A nucleotide has three parts: a pentose sugar, a nitrogenous base and a phosphate group. The sugar and base alone make a nucleoside, and adding the phosphate makes it a nucleotide.

why_wrong.0: Sugar plus base is a nucleoside. This is the distinction the question is testing, and the phosphate is what completes it.
why_wrong.1: Sugar plus phosphate forms the backbone of the chain, but without a base it carries no genetic information.
why_wrong.3: Base plus phosphate is not a recognised unit. The sugar is what links the two together.

why_correct: Amino acids join through peptide bonds, formed between the carboxyl group of one and the amino group of the next with the loss of a water molecule.

why_wrong.0: Glycosidic bonds link sugars into polysaccharides such as starch and cellulose.
why_wrong.1: Phosphodiester bonds link nucleotides into DNA and RNA.
why_wrong.3: Hydrogen bonds do hold proteins in shape, giving the alpha helix and beta sheet, but they are weak interactions and not what joins the amino acids in sequence.

why_correct: Prokaryotic ribosomes are 70S, made of a 50S large subunit and a 30S small one. The S values do not add up arithmetically because they measure sedimentation rate, which depends on shape as well as mass.

why_wrong.0: 80S ribosomes are found in eukaryotic cytoplasm. This is the pair to remember: 70S prokaryotic, 80S eukaryotic.
why_wrong.2: 60S is the large subunit of the eukaryotic 80S ribosome, not a whole ribosome.
why_wrong.3: 50S is the large subunit of the prokaryotic ribosome, so it is a part of the answer rather than the answer.

why_correct: Mitochondria are the site of aerobic respiration. The Krebs cycle runs in the matrix and the electron transport chain sits in the inner membrane, which is why they are called the powerhouse of the cell.

why_wrong.0: Chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis, which stores energy rather than releasing it, and they occur only in plants.
why_wrong.1: The endoplasmic reticulum handles protein and lipid synthesis and transport.
why_wrong.3: The nucleolus makes ribosomal RNA. Note that glycolysis, the first stage of respiration, happens in the cytoplasm, but the aerobic stages are mitochondrial.

why_correct: Lysosomes are called suicide bags because they are full of hydrolytic enzymes that can digest the cell's own contents if the membrane bursts. They also digest worn-out organelles and engulfed material.

why_wrong.0: The Golgi apparatus packages and dispatches proteins, and it is in fact where lysosomes are formed, which makes it a tempting answer.
why_wrong.2: Mitochondria release energy and do have a role in programmed cell death, but they are not enzyme sacs.
why_wrong.3: Ribosomes build proteins and have no membrane at all, so they could not contain enzymes in this way.

why_correct: Singer and Nicolson proposed the fluid mosaic model in 1972, describing the membrane as a lipid bilayer in which proteins float like a mosaic and can move laterally.

why_wrong.0: Schleiden and Schwann gave the cell theory, that all plants and animals are made of cells.
why_wrong.2: Robert Hooke first saw and named cells, in a slice of cork in 1665.
why_wrong.3: Anton von Leeuwenhoek first observed living microorganisms with his own lenses. All three wrong options are much earlier, and membrane structure is a twentieth-century question.

why_correct: The frog's heart has three chambers: two atria and a single ventricle. Because the ventricle is undivided, oxygenated and deoxygenated blood mix to some extent, which is typical of amphibians.

why_wrong.1: One atrium with two ventricles occurs in no vertebrate. It is the atria that are paired first in evolution.
why_wrong.2: Two atria and two ventricles is the four-chambered heart of birds, mammals and crocodiles, which keeps the two bloodstreams completely separate.
why_wrong.3: A single atrium with a single ventricle is the two-chambered heart of fishes.

why_correct: Tendons and ligaments are dense connective tissue, in which collagen fibres are packed tightly and lie parallel. That arrangement gives great tensile strength in one direction.

why_wrong.0: Loose connective tissue, such as areolar tissue, has fibres scattered in abundant ground substance and fills spaces rather than bearing loads.
why_wrong.2: Specialised connective tissue covers cartilage, bone, blood and adipose tissue.
why_wrong.3: Vascular tissue in animals means blood and lymph. Note the difference between the two: tendons join muscle to bone, ligaments join bone to bone.

why_correct: In a monocot stem the vascular bundles are scattered through the ground tissue and are closed, meaning they contain no cambium. Without cambium the stem cannot grow in thickness.

why_wrong.0: Open means cambium is present, which is a dicot feature. Scattered is right but open is wrong.
why_wrong.2: Open and in a ring describes the dicot stem exactly, so this is the opposite of the answer.
why_wrong.3: Closed is right but the ring is wrong. Take the two properties separately: scattered against ringed, and closed against open.

why_correct: Lateral meristem, that is the vascular and cork cambium, produces secondary growth and so increases the girth of the stem.

why_wrong.0: Apical meristem sits at the tips of root and shoot and increases length, not girth.
why_wrong.1: Intercalary meristem lies at the base of internodes, notably in grasses, and also adds length. It is why a lawn regrows after mowing.
why_wrong.3: Parenchyma is a simple permanent tissue, not a meristem, so it does not divide to add new tissue.

why_correct: In the pea the upper leaflets of the compound leaf are modified into tendrils, so it climbs by leaf tendrils. The rest of the leaf still photosynthesises.

why_wrong.0: Stem tendrils are found in plants such as the grapevine and passion flower, where the tendril arises in the axil rather than from the leaf.
why_wrong.2: The pea's roots are ordinary except for their nitrogen-fixing nodules, and they play no part in climbing.
why_wrong.3: Only one of these is true of the pea, so all of these is wrong.

why_correct: The potato belongs to Solanaceae, the nightshade family, along with tomato, brinjal, chilli and tobacco. The edible potato is a stem tuber, not a root.

why_wrong.0: Fabaceae is the pea and bean family, whose members bear pods and fix nitrogen.
why_wrong.2: Liliaceae is the lily family, which includes onion and garlic.
why_wrong.3: Poaceae is the grass family, which includes rice, wheat and maize.

why_correct: Inflorescence is the arrangement of flowers on the floral axis, and it is classified as racemose, cymose and so on according to how the axis grows.

why_wrong.0: Phyllotaxy is the arrangement of leaves on the stem, which is the same idea applied to leaves instead of flowers.
why_wrong.1: Placentation is the arrangement of ovules inside the ovary.
why_wrong.3: Venation is the pattern of veins in a leaf, reticulate in dicots and parallel in monocots.

why_correct: Pneumatic bones, hollow and filled with air spaces connected to the lungs, are found in Aves. They reduce weight without much loss of strength and are one of the key adaptations for flight.

why_wrong.0: Amphibians have solid bones and no flight adaptations.
why_wrong.1: Reptiles likewise have solid bones. Some extinct flying reptiles had air spaces, but the class as a whole does not.
why_wrong.3: Mammals have solid bones, including bats, which fly with membranes and light limb bones but not pneumatic ones.

why_correct: Annelids show true metameric segmentation, in which the body is divided into a series of similar segments both externally and internally. The earthworm is the standard example.

why_wrong.0: Platyhelminthes, the flatworms, are unsegmented, though tapeworms have repeating proglottids, which is a superficial resemblance rather than true segmentation.
why_wrong.1: Aschelminthes, the roundworms, are unsegmented and have a pseudocoelom.
why_wrong.3: Coelenterates such as Hydra and jellyfish have radial symmetry and no segmentation at all.

why_correct: The water vascular system, a network of canals ending in tube feet, is unique to Echinodermata. Starfish use it for locomotion, feeding and gas exchange.

why_wrong.0: Porifera, the sponges, have a canal system of ostia and oscula for feeding, which is a different structure with a different purpose.
why_wrong.1: Ctenophora, the comb jellies, move by rows of ciliary plates.
why_wrong.3: Chordates have a closed blood vascular system, not a water vascular one.

why_correct: In pteridophytes the sporophyte is the dominant, independent, photosynthetic plant, with true roots, stem and leaves. This is the reverse of bryophytes, where the gametophyte dominates.

why_wrong.0: The gametophyte in ferns is the small, short-lived prothallus, quite unlike the conspicuous fern plant.
why_wrong.2: The prothallus is that gametophyte, so it is the same wrong answer named differently.
why_wrong.3: The protonema is a juvenile stage of the moss gametophyte, belonging to bryophytes rather than pteridophytes.

why_correct: Gymnosperm means naked seed. Their ovules are not enclosed in an ovary, so the seeds sit exposed on the scales of a cone, as in pine and cycad.

why_wrong.0: Angiosperms are the flowering plants, whose seeds are enclosed in a fruit developed from the ovary. Angio means vessel, which is the exact contrast.
why_wrong.2: Pteridophytes, the ferns, produce spores and no seeds at all.
why_wrong.3: Bryophytes, the mosses and liverworts, also reproduce by spores.

why_correct: A lichen is a symbiosis of an alga and a fungus. The alga photosynthesises and feeds the partnership, while the fungus provides shelter, anchorage, water and minerals.

why_wrong.0: Viruses cannot live in symbiosis; they are obligate parasites and are not cellular.
why_wrong.2: Fungi with the roots of higher plants form mycorrhiza, a different and equally important symbiosis. That is the classic distractor here.
why_wrong.3: Lichens are indeed excellent bio-indicators of air quality, but that is a use we make of them, not the partnership they are made of.

why_correct: R. H. Whittaker proposed the five kingdom system in 1969: Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia. He used cell structure, body organisation and mode of nutrition as the criteria.

why_wrong.0: Carl Woese proposed the three domain system in 1990, adding Archaea as a separate domain.
why_wrong.1: Ernst Mayr gave the biological species concept, defining a species by interbreeding.
why_wrong.3: Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin, which is microbiology rather than taxonomy.

why_correct: Monera contains all the prokaryotes, that is bacteria, cyanobacteria, mycoplasma and archaebacteria. They have no true nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles.

why_wrong.0: Protista holds single-celled eukaryotes such as Amoeba, Paramecium and Euglena. Single-celled but nucleated, which is the distinction being tested.
why_wrong.2: Fungi are eukaryotes with cell walls of chitin.
why_wrong.3: Plantae are multicellular eukaryotes with cellulose walls and chlorophyll.
